title: Good Data, Bad Data
desc: Clean and sort data to see how the quality of data shapes what AI learns
content_html:
What We're Doing

AI learns from data, so the data has to be fair and complete for the AI to be any good. Bad data in means bad decisions out — an AI can only ever be as good as what it learns from. In this lesson we gather some data ourselves, then deliberately break it, so we can see exactly how gaps and bias in the data become gaps and bias in the AI.

You'll Need

  • A whiteboard or paper to tally results
  • A simple question to survey the class (for example "What is your favourite fruit?")
  • Optional: a few printed photos or a short list to act as a "training set" to sort

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Run a quick survey of the whole class and tally the results on the board. This is our "good" dataset — everyone got a say.
  2. Interrogate the data together: Did everyone get to answer? Was anyone away or skipped? Is any group over- or under-counted?
  3. Now break it on purpose: imagine you only asked the front two rows. Predict how the result would change, then discuss why that sample is unfair.
  4. Connect it to AI: if this biased survey trained an AI to "guess the class's favourite fruit", what wrong thing would it learn?
  5. As a group, brainstorm three rules for collecting fairer, more complete data next time.

Examples

  • A face-unlock trained mostly on one skin tone works poorly for everyone else.
  • A voice assistant trained on one accent keeps mishearing people who speak differently.
  • A "best student" predictor trained only on past winners quietly repeats old unfairness.

Facilitation Tips

  • Let learners discover the bias themselves by asking "who is missing?" rather than telling them.
  • Keep the fruit example light, then pivot hard to the real-world examples so the stakes land.
  • Emphasise that bad data is usually an honest mistake, not villainy — which is why checking is everyone's job.

Discussion Questions

  • What does "fair and complete" data actually mean for a dataset?
  • How could a company end up with biased data without meaning to?
  • If you found an AI was trained on unfair data, what would you do about it?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Clean a deliberately messy list (duplicates, blanks, typos) and explain each fix.
  • Medium: Find a real news story about AI bias and summarise what data caused it.
  • Hard: Design a data-collection plan for a fair "favourite school lunch" predictor — who you'd ask, how many, and how you'd avoid bias.
